1:
Delitzsch sets the psalm beside the one before it as a contrast, that being cheerful and this the gloomiest of all the plaintive psalms — not Psalm 77, which the old expositors named when asked which ode was saddest. The name God of my salvation shows the spark of faith is not quite out, but nothing else brightens: the gloom never rises into hope, and the psalm dies away in Job-like lamentation. Henry says the same from the other side: the very first words are the only words of comfort in the whole psalm, there is nothing about the writer but clouds and darkness, and Heman, a seer and a comforter of others, could see no comfort for himself. Spurgeon calls the title the one ray of light: while a man can see God as his Saviour it is not altogether midnight with him.

Who wrote it, and out of what trouble, nobody settles. Clarke would translate the title as a poem sung responsively on behalf of a distressed person, reports Kennicott's view that it is the prayer of a leper shut up in a separate house in the last stage of the disease and Calmet's that it belongs to the captivity, and works out the genealogy by which Heman and Ethan are grandsons of Judah — which, if true, would make these the oldest poems extant. Then he throws the enquiry over: to labour at reconciling the psalm titles is to treat them with too much respect, since many are wrongly placed and none are inspired. Calvin collects the same options — Kennicott's leper, Kimchi's captive speaking as a slave under his chains, Bishop Patrick's dark prison — without deciding among them.

Augustine takes the opposite view of titles, reading this one as the psalm's subject. The phrase he finds nowhere else he renders for the chorus, and hears in it the Passion: Christ goes before as precentor and the choir of martyrs takes up the strain, which is what responding means. The sons of Korah are the imitators of that Passion, Korah being for him the interpretation of Calvary. But the choir signifies concord, and concord consists in charity — so a man may give his body to be burnt and still not answer in the choir, and it profits him nothing.

What Calvin draws from the authorship is use, not history. God exercised Heman, whom he had adorned with such gifts, not for his servant's sake only: Heman mounts an elevated stage and testifies to the whole Church his infirmities along with his faith, so that our own distresses may not overwhelm us when we see how hard even he laboured to emerge from that darkness into the light of hope. The psalm is therefore a form of prayer put into the mouths of the afflicted who stand on the brink. The brief opening is a bridle the poet lays on himself, lest the heat of his feelings carry him into murmuring instead of supplication; most men complain under grief, but few pour their groanings out before God, and it is a rare virtue to set him before our eyes at all.

Gill hears in God of my salvation both temporal and spiritual deliverance, and notes the faith behind it was never so low that the psalmist could not still call the Lord his own — as Christ, forsaken, still called him his God. Spurgeon works the second half: distress had not blown out the sparks of the prayer but quickened them, till they burned like a furnace at full blast. Had the pain not been incessant the supplication might have been intermittent, so it is well that sickness will not let us rest if we spend the restlessness in prayer. Both hours suit prayer — go with Daniel and pray where men can see, and with Jacob wrestle at Jabbok till the day breaks.
2:
Clarke's note on verse 2 turns into the longest excursus in the chapter. The prayer he calls weak and helpless though fervent and sincere, wanting only that the hindrances be taken out of its way; then he transcribes what he considers one of the finest thoughts in the Iliad. Prayers there are the daughters of Jove, wrinkled and lame and slant-eyed, who follow limping after Offence — and Offence is robust and firm of foot, outstripping them all and running over the earth hurting men, while they come after and heal the hurt. Received respectfully, they give aid; refused, they cry to Jove that offence may cleave to the man for vengeance. The translator's gloss is that they are wrinkled because the face of a man driven to prayer by a consciousness of guilt is a sorrowful one. Gill keeps the temple image: the prayer is not to be shut out but to ascend perfumed with the much incense of the mediation.

Ellicott supplies the argument that holds the section together. Sheol severs the covenant relation with God, and that is the irresistible reason why the prayer must be heard now, before it is too late. Working verse by verse he prefers a hero whose strength is gone to a man that hath no strength, reads pressed me down with all thy breakers in verse 7, and takes the shutting up of verse 8 as figure rather than actual imprisonment, with a page of Job before the poet. Delitzsch hears Job too — the complaint about the alienation of his nearest relations sounds like Job 19, though the same strain runs through the earlier psalms of suffering.

Free among the dead is the crux, and no two agree. Ellicott reports that the old versions without exception take the word as an adjective, as it is used of an emancipated slave, of freedom from public burdens, and of the separate house in which a leprous king was cut off from society — which is why some refer the psalm to Uzziah — while the Targum explains it as freed from legal duties. He holds the sense is plainly that of the Latin defunctus, and records that Gesenius makes the word a noun and renders among the dead is my couch. Clarke would rather read stripped among the dead, taking verses 4 and 5 for a field of battle where the spoilers strip not only the dead but the mortally wounded too feeble to resist. Wesley keeps the received sense: well nigh discharged from the warfare of this life and entered as a member into the society of the dead. Gill hears one who thought himself as neglected as a corpse.

Two readings run past the verse. Clarke notes that the fathers applied free among the dead to Christ's voluntary death: all others are obliged to die and are bound in the grave, but he alone laid down his life and could take it again. On cut off from thy hand he sees the roll in which a general enters every man of his army, from which the killed are erased and written into a separate book — the black book, or book of death, against the book of life where the living are enrolled. He observes drily that from this circumstance the doctrine of unconditional reprobation and election has been derived, and leaves it at how wonderful.

By verse 9 the eye is failing. Ellicott renders it fadeth or pineth, quoting a Latin poet on eyes wasting under continual weeping. Delitzsch marks the turn there: the man who complains like this without knowing any comfort, and yet without despairing, gathers himself up afresh for prayer, and his complaints are themselves petitions, since they are poured out before God. The destiny under which he has long been more like one dying than living reaches back, he adds, into the man's youth.
10:
The questions of verses 10 to 12 are rhetorical, and Clarke says the interrogations imply the strongest negations. Ellicott insists they are not about resurrection as we understand it, since that hope had hardly dawned on Israel: the underworld is one vast sepulchre where the dead lie each in his place, and the poet asks how they could rise to praise a God who has forgotten them. The word he renders shades is used elsewhere of the giant races of Palestine, but here means the dead — languid shapes lying supine, cut off from the upper air, yet retaining sensation enough to feel the gloomy monotony of death. Lovingkindness here means covenant grace, and faithfulness, wonders and righteousness are limited the same way: death severed the covenant, and the grave knew nothing of it.

Henry will not read the passage as despair, or as disbelieving the last resurrection; it pleads for speedy relief. Departed souls may declare God's faithfulness, but deceased bodies can neither receive his favours in comfort nor return them in praise. Gill finds the wonders granted after all: God shows them to the dead in trespasses by quickening them, and showed them to Christ before he saw corruption. Clarke takes the second question as doctrine: faithfulness covers God's threatenings as much as his promises, but annihilation is no punishment, so he cannot mean to annihilate the wicked. On the land of forgetfulness he notes the heathen had some notion of it, feigning the river Lethe. Wesley puts it shortest: the grave, where men are forgotten by their nearest relations.

Verse 13 turns. Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic — but as for me — the speaker has not gone down to the land where all is forgotten and can still cry, which sharpens what follows, since a man alive and inside the covenant is asking why he is forsaken. Clarke glosses prevent as get before thee: he will not wait for the usual hour of morning sacrifice. Henry turns it round: God often prevents our prayers with his mercies, and we should prevent his mercies with our prayers.

The last strophe is unrelieved. Ellicott finds loathing in the verb of verse 14, a throwing away with disgust. Henry says nothing grieves a child of God so much as this hiding of the face: if the sun be clouded that darkens the earth, but if the sun abandoned the earth altogether, what a dungeon would it be. On the terrors Ellicott counts another link with Job, and puzzles at the word rendered distracted, which occurs nowhere else — the versions soften it to a general word for trouble, but the context wants more, and a cognate meaning wheel might give I turn giddy, or one altered stroke I grow frigid. Clarke observes that where the terrors of the Lord prevail there is neither health of body nor peace of mind. Henry allows that even those designed for God's favours may for a time suffer his terrors, the spirit of adoption being first a spirit of bondage to fear, and that Heman's reason was nearly taken from him.

The closing word is bleakest. Ellicott calls the received rendering wrong: not mine acquaintance into darkness but darkness is my friend, having taken the place of those removed — beside which he sets Tennyson's sorrow that would live with him as a wife. Clarke reaches the same phrase — darkness is my companion — and says that man has a dismal lot who has outlived his old friends and sees in their removal little but the triumphs of death, quoting the Persian poet whose echo answers Where are they with the same words. Henry ends there too: next to the comforts of religion are those of friendship, so to be friendless is almost to be comfortless — the finishing stroke of the melancholy piece. Gill hears the disciples who forsook Christ.
